text:
Part 1: Context

Background

The Government’s strategy, A National Plan to End Homelessness (December 2025), sets out a cross-government commitment to get back on track to ending all forms of homelessness. The Prime Minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping builds on the actions set out in the strategy, supported by record levels of investment in homelessness and rough sleeping services over the next three years.

As part of this commitment, the Department for Education (DfE) and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) published the Care leaver homelessness reduction action plan in November 2026 to reduce homelessness among care leavers. The plan focuses on earlier preparation for leaving care, stronger local authority practice, access to suitable and sustainable housing, enduring relationships with trusted adults, and innovative housing models that strengthen connection and belonging.

This guide provides practical support to help local authorities and their partners strengthen housing pathways, improve accommodation outcomes for care leavers, and prevent homelessness. The homelessness system should never be used as a planned accommodation pathway for young people leaving care. Local authorities should work proactively with partners to ensure safe, suitable and sustainable accommodation is in place before a young person leaves care.

This principle should extend beyond the initial transition from care. Care leavers can face housing instability and homelessness at later transition points, including when moving on from supported accommodation, Staying Put arrangements or other forms of housing support. Local authorities and partners should therefore plan ahead at each transition point, to minimise the risk of homelessness and avoid reliance on the homelessness system as a route to accommodation.

Executive summary

Care-experienced young people face a significantly higher risk of homelessness and housing instability than their peers. Safe, stable and suitable housing is fundamental to a successful transition to adulthood, supporting education, employment, health, wellbeing, relationships and a sense of belonging.

Preventing homelessness requires early, proactive planning, with housing needs identified well before a young person leaves care and clear pathways into appropriate accommodation. Support should be flexible and responsive as needs change, recognising that transitions to independence are rarely linear and that young people may need to re-engage with support following setbacks.

There is no single housing solution that will meet the needs of every care leaver. Local authorities should therefore provide a diverse range of accommodation and support options, offering genuine choice and enabling young people to adapt to new circumstances at the right pace. Across all pathways, the aim should be to provide the right home, in the right place, at the right time, alongside enduring relationships and practical support that help care leavers sustain their accommodation and thrive into adulthood.

One care leaver said:

feeling safe in your neighbourhood and home shouldn’t be a luxury but some care experienced individuals might believe it to be… a secure and stable home would encourage young people to build foundations they’ll need to thrive through education, employment or other things they want to do.[footnote 1]

Strong corporate parenting should underpin all housing decisions for care leavers. Achieving positive housing outcomes requires shared responsibility across children’s services, housing, homelessness, education, health and wider partners, with effective joint working, clear governance and accountability to prevent young people falling between services.

Local authorities should use the guide to strengthen housing pathways and local offers, plan for future accommodation demand, secure sufficient suitable housing and invest in early intervention, homelessness prevention and tenancy sustainment. Effective pathways should combine a diverse range of accommodation with consistent, relationship-based support.

Housing cannot be considered in isolation. Accommodation, health and wellbeing, education, employment, finances, relationships and community connections are closely linked and should form part of a coordinated pathway to adulthood. Personal Advisers have a key role in helping care leavers navigate services, maintain important relationships and access support as their circumstances change.

About this guide

This guide has been informed by a series of deep dive discussions that the Department for Education held with local authorities and other organisations that support care leavers. Through these deep dives, participating local authorities and partner organisations shared their experiences, challenges, and examples of emerging practice in supporting care leavers with housing. Part 3 of this guide contains examples of housing pathways that are drawn from those discussions.

This guide is intended for:

children’s services

leaving care teams

housing authorities

housing commissioners

corporate parenting boards (which bring together senior local leaders, local authority managers and staff, and care experienced young people)

wider partner organisations, which may all be involved in planning, commissioning or delivering accommodation and support for care leavers.

It is intended to provide practical insights to inform thinking and planning and help develop or review local housing offers for care leavers, rather than prescribing a definitive model of delivery, as local housing markets, resources, and young people’s needs will differ from area to area across the country.

Placing enduring relationships at the centre of children’s social care

Enduring relationships are the stable, trusted relationships that give care experienced young people emotional security, support, and a sense of belonging. Defined by the young person, enduring relationships may include family members, foster carers, friends, teachers, personal advisers, or other trusted adults. The Enduring Relationships Strategy puts these relationships at the centre of children’s social care, recognising that even one reliable adult can improve outcomes, build resilience, and support wellbeing. The care system can disrupt important connections, so the emphasis must be on the need to help young people stay connected to family, friends, and communities wherever it is safe and appropriate.

One care leaver said:

My brother is my best friend and the only person in my family. Love him more than myself.[footnote 2]

Placement and accommodation decisions should consider not only the quality of the home, but also the impact on the relationships that matter most to the young person. Enduring relationships can play a critical role in preventing homelessness by providing emotional support, practical advice, advocacy and early intervention when difficulties arise. Trusted adults and supportive networks act as informal safety nets, helping young people sustain tenancies, navigate crises, access services and avoid social isolation.

One young person said:

My mum and dad are dead, but I have a strong bond with my nana.[footnote 3]

By supporting care leavers to develop and maintain lasting relationships, local authorities can strengthen resilience, improve housing stability and reduce the risk of homelessness and rough sleeping as young people transition to adulthood. They should therefore consider a young person’s relationship network as a core component of effective housing pathways.

Approaches such as Staying Close, Family Finding, Lifelong Links and relationship-focused pathway planning can help ensure that care leavers enter adulthood with a sustained network of support around them.

Care leaver local offer

The Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 strengthens requirements on housing and financial wellbeing in local authorities’ local offers for care leavers. Local authorities must set out how they will anticipate accommodation needs, prevent homelessness and help care leavers, including those leaving custody, access and sustain suitable housing.

The local offer must also provide clear information on housing pathways, tenancy and financial support, and financial entitlements, alongside support to develop financial literacy and manage budgeting, benefits, banking, debt and savings.

The guidance Care leaver local offer: guidance for local authorities (effective from 30 September 2026) was published in August 2026 and duties came into force on 30 September 2026.

Corporate parenting responsibilities

The corporate parenting principles, introduced through the Children and Social Work Act 2017, require local authorities to support looked after children and care leavers as a good parent would for their child. This is a whole-authority responsibility, including housing, homelessness, education and health services.

Stable, suitable and affordable housing is central to good corporate parenting, providing the secure foundation care leavers need to develop skills and confidence while remaining connected to the relationships and support networks that enable healthy interdependence, and access education, employment and support. This means not only providing accommodation, but ensuring it is safe, appropriate and supported.

Corporate parenting is also key to preventing homelessness. Local authorities should plan ahead, intervene early and embed prevention through pathway planning, a range of housing options, strong joint working between housing and leaving care services, and proactive tenancy sustainment support. This can improve housing stability and reduce the risk of homelessness.

Providing the right housing to avoid homelessness and achieve housing stability

A successful transition to adulthood for care experienced young people involves more than simply securing accommodation. Care experienced young people have emphasised that housing stability is about having a home, not a placement.

One care leaver said:

Professionals could be more understanding and allow [care leavers] to have options about where they live, how they furnish their house, and the area they live in.[footnote 4]

Housing stability depends on access to the right support. This includes help with budgeting, cooking, cleaning, self-care and tenancy sustainment. Young people highlight the value of trusted adults, peer mentors and positive role models. Young people stress that a home needs to feel personal and valued, rather than somewhere they have been placed because there was no other option.

One young person reflected:

A lot of the reason somewhere does not feel like home is when young people are made to feel like an obligation. Time-limited accommodation can also make it difficult to settle, put down roots and develop a sense of belonging.

Difficulties with mental health can increase the risk of tenancy breakdown, homelessness and social isolation, while unstable accommodation can negatively affect emotional wellbeing and recovery.

One care leaver said:

I am not living near family and support without having to travel for a long period of time, this is hard because I am disabled… my mental health has had a massive decline since living here but there’s nothing I can do except hope and pray that I can get a mutual exchange out of here and closer to my family and support…[footnote 5]

Local authorities should ensure that housing pathways are supported by access to appropriate emotional wellbeing and mental health services, including clear referral routes into specialist support where needed.

The housing that care experienced young people receive should offer safety, belonging, dignity, and the opportunity to build a stable future.

Matching accommodation to need

Matching accommodation to a young person’s individual needs is essential to preventing homelessness and sustaining tenancies. Care leavers have different experiences, strengths and vulnerabilities, and housing decisions should reflect these.

This includes recognising risks arising from domestic abuse, neglect or family harm, where returning to particular situations, communities or areas may expose young people to further harm or re-traumatisation. Safe accommodation, specialist support, advocacy and help to relocate should be available where needed.

For young people leaving custody, secure settings or other institutions, housing planning should begin well before release or discharge, with agencies working together to ensure appropriate accommodation and support are in place and reduce the risk of homelessness, isolation and disrupted support.

Housing decisions should also support young people’s wider aspirations and long-term outcomes, including education, training, employment, relationships and developing the skills needed in adulthood.

Local authorities should provide a range of options, including Staying Put, stepping stone and supported accommodation, foyers, social housing, private rented accommodation and specialist provision, enabling young people to progress out of care well supported, at a pace that is right for them.

Effective pathway planning, tenancy sustainment support and early intervention are key to preventing tenancy breakdown and homelessness.

Young people should be actively involved in these decisions and, wherever possible, offered genuine choice between suitable options that reflect their needs, aspirations and support networks.

Part 2: Developing and delivering housing pathways for care leavers

Joint protocols: roles and responsibilities

Joint housing protocols for care leavers are formal agreements between children’s services, housing authorities and other partners that set out how they will work together to meet the accommodation needs of care leavers and prevent homelessness.

They support local authorities to fulfil their corporate parenting responsibilities by promoting shared accountability for securing positive housing outcomes and ensuring care leavers can access and sustain suitable accommodation.

Effective protocols establish clear roles, information-sharing arrangements and joint working practices, helping services identify and address housing risks early and ensuring care leavers do not fall between systems.

Protocols should be supported by strong governance, data scrutiny, regular review, senior oversight and lessons from young people’s lived experience, to maintain joint ownership across housing and children’s services and monitor outcomes for care leavers.

To prevent tenancy breakdown, joint protocols should support early identification of risks (such as rent arrears, neighbour disputes, disengagement from support, poor mental health, domestic abuse, exploitation and anti-social behaviour), with housing, children’s services, leaving care teams and providers working together to intervene early and prevent avoidable eviction or unplanned loss of accommodation.

Through coordinated support, early intervention and shared responsibility, joint housing protocols are one of the most effective mechanisms for preventing care leaver homelessness, improving housing stability and demonstrating effective corporate parenting. Guidance on joint housing protocols can be found in Joint housing protocols for care leavers.

Governance arrangements

Providing a range of effective housing pathway options for care leavers requires strong partnership working between children’s services, housing teams, and wider housing providers, supported by clear governance and identification of housing risks.

Housing commissioning teams should work closely with children’s services to assess current and future demand and ensure sufficient provision of appropriate accommodation and support services for care leavers. Local authorities should also work with registered providers and housing associations to improve access to stable and affordable housing and support care leavers to sustain their tenancies.

Partnerships with private landlords should be developed and strengthened wherever appropriate. This may include use of rent deposit schemes, rent guarantee arrangements, landlord incentive programmes, and dedicated tenancy sustainment support.

Ongoing engagement with landlords can help build confidence, address concerns at an early stage, and support successful tenancies.

Where a care-experienced young person is at significant risk of tenancy breakdown, homelessness, or rough sleeping, local authorities should consider convening a multi-agency case conference involving senior representatives from children’s services, housing authorities, and relevant housing providers. The purpose of the meeting should be to review risks, consider corporate parenting responsibilities, identify additional preventative action, and agree a coordinated plan with the young person wherever possible.

Local authorities should establish clear escalation routes and shared accountability arrangements to ensure housing issues are addressed promptly and effectively.

Strong partnership working can improve tenancy sustainment, prevent avoidable homelessness, and ensure care leavers receive coordinated support at the right time.

Understanding future demand and sufficiency

In order to understand future demand and sufficiency of housing and accommodation for care leavers, Ofsted’s research How local authorities plan for sufficiency of accommodation that meets the needs of children in care and care leavers suggests that local authorities should combine demographic and care-leaver forecasting with intelligence from housing services, providers, and regional partners.

The focus should be on predicting future need, identifying gaps in provision early, and ensuring the right mix of accommodation and support is available to help care leavers achieve stability and positive outcomes.

Effective planning requires close relationships with housing services, health partners, accommodation providers, and neighbouring authorities to ensure demand is understood across the local system and to identify gaps in provision early. Future housing demand should be incorporated into wider commissioning and placement strategies.

Local authorities are required to produce and publish Local Supported Housing Strategies under the Supported Housing (Regulatory Oversight) Act 2023.

These strategies provide an opportunity for local authorities to assess the current and future accommodation and support needs of care leavers, including the sufficiency of local provision, gaps in supported housing pathways, and the support needed to help care leavers move successfully towards independent living.

Local authorities should recognise where wider system factors may limit the availability of housing pathways for care leavers. These may include, for example, shortages of social housing, or affordability pressures within local housing markets.

Sufficiency assessments and housing pathway planning should therefore identify these barriers, consider their likely impact on care leavers, and explore mitigating actions such as strengthened tenancy sustainment support, rent guarantor and deposit schemes, regional commissioning arrangements, enhanced allocation policies, and engagement with local landlords.

Local authorities should use homelessness statistics (H-CLIC) and ensure joint scrutiny of data across housing and children’s services, shared ownership of data quality, and the use of journey analysis alongside lived experience to support continued learning, the strengthening of protocols and improvements to joint practice.

Regular reporting of these trends should inform decision making, support early identification of risks, and help ensure that changes in practice lead to measurable improvements in outcomes for care-experienced young people. For guidance on developing joint housing protocols, see Joint housing protocols for care leavers

Local authorities shaping the market

Effective market shaping combines increasing housing supply with practical support to help care-experienced young people secure and sustain stable accommodation. Local authorities can use a mix of social housing, supported and transitional accommodation, supported lodgings and the private rented sector.

Housing allocation policies can support care leavers through priority access to social housing and clear move-on routes. Local authorities must give reasonable preference to certain groups, including people who are homeless or need to move on welfare or hardship grounds, and can award additional preference where housing needs are urgent. See Social housing allocations guidance .

Local authorities should also consider specialist provision that reflects local need. Where demand is low, joint or regional commissioning can help create sufficient scale, improve choice and sustain specialist accommodation. Planning powers, housing partnerships, council-owned properties and local housing companies can also help increase affordable supply.

Access to the private rented sector can be improved through rent guarantor schemes, deposit assistance and rent-in-advance payments, alongside engagement with landlords and letting agents and ongoing tenancy support. Further information on rent guarantor and deposit schemes is provided in Part 3 of this guide.

Importance of early assessment and pathway planning from age 16

The Children Act 1989 Guidance and Regulations: Volume 3, Planning Transition to Adulthood for Care Leavers makes clear that housing and accommodation planning should begin well before a young person leaves care and should form part of wider transition planning from age 16, and often earlier.

Accommodation needs should be assessed through pathway planning and reflected in the young person’s pathway plan alongside their education, employment, health and wider wellbeing needs. Local authorities should provide planned, progressive housing pathways that support a gradual move towards adulthood, rather than crisis-led moves, with appropriate tenancy sustainment support.

Pathway plans should identify suitable accommodation, support needs and contingency arrangements. Early identification of issues and action are essential to preventing escalation.

Providers and young people should have clear routes and named contacts for raising concerns, including rent arrears, repairs, conflict, exploitation, distress or difficulties managing daily life, with agreed notification arrangements across relevant services. Concerns should be recorded including any immediate risks and the timeframe for action, so that partners can respond to early warning signs before issues escalate to crisis point.

For care leavers in education or training, local authorities should prioritise accommodation stability and minimise disruption to learning. Where a move is being considered, its impact on education should be carefully assessed and, except where safeguarding or exceptional circumstances require it, planned moves should wherever possible take place at the end of the academic year.

Young people should be fully involved in decisions about any move, with appropriate support in place to minimise disruption to their education and progress.

Pathway planning and accommodation discussions should support second chances. Previous rent arrears, missed appointments or tenancy breakdown should prompt consideration of the underlying circumstances and what additional support or alternative accommodation may be needed, rather than automatically restricting access to future housing opportunities.

Contingency planning for young people at higher risk of accommodation breakdown

For care leavers at greater risk of accommodation breakdown, including those presenting with multiple and complex needs, joint contingency planning should form part of the pathway plan and wider accommodation planning before a crisis occurs to prevent risk of homelessness.

This should build on known risks, needs and previous experiences, including placement instability, complex or overlapping support needs, limited support networks, safeguarding concerns or experience of the criminal justice system.

To mitigate this risk, the pathway plan should identify early warning signs, the action that housing, children’s services, accommodation providers and other partners will take to sustain the existing arrangement, and how concerns will be escalated where risks increase.

One key intervention that children’s services can offer young people as they prepare to leave care is support to move to a new home through Staying Close.

The Staying Close programme is being rolled out nationally in a phased approach, ahead of the Staying Close duty coming into force in 2029.

Where accommodation cannot be sustained, services should agree how a managed move or suitable alternative accommodation and continued support will be provided, to avoid homelessness and risk of rough sleeping, and reliance on homelessness services wherever possible. Contingency arrangements should be developed with the young person and reviewed when their circumstances or accommodation change.

Local authorities should ensure that young people at risk of tenancy breakdown are considered for available homelessness prevention and tenancy sustainment services at the earliest opportunity. This should include consideration of tenancy rescue, early help and other targeted interventions aimed at preventing avoidable evictions and homelessness.

Information sharing

The Children Act 1989 Guidance and Regulations: Volume 3, Planning Transition to Adulthood for Care Leavers makes clear that effective support for care leavers depends on effective information sharing between children’s services, housing authorities and other relevant partners. Local authorities should ensure that information-sharing arrangements support coordinated assessment, pathway planning, accommodation planning and homelessness prevention. Information-sharing expectations should be reflected in local joint protocols and partnership arrangements to promote effective joint working.

Working across local authority boundaries

Local authorities should work collaboratively to ensure care leavers receive seamless support across boundaries. Accommodation decisions should prioritise safety, wellbeing, support networks, education and employment, with cross-boundary moves planned to maintain continuity of support.

Part 3: Accommodation options

Staying Put

Staying Put is a statutory arrangement that enables young people who were looked after in foster care to remain living with their former foster carers beyond the age of 18 where this supports their welfare and transition to adulthood. Local authorities should view Staying Put as a core component of their accommodation offer for care leavers.

Staying Put should not be viewed solely as an extension of a foster placement. It is a vital part of a local authority’s corporate parenting responsibilities and a key tool for improving outcomes for care leavers.

As part of a wider accommodation pathway and homelessness prevention strategy, effective Staying Put provision can help ensure more care leavers move into adulthood from a position of stability, readiness and support, rather than housing crisis and instability.

Why Staying Put matters

For many care leavers, turning 18 does not mean they are ready to live independently. Staying Put provides continuity, stability and ongoing support at a critical stage of a young person’s life. It enables young people to maintain trusted relationships, continue developing independence skills, and make a gradual and planned transition to adulthood.

Evidence indicates that stable accommodation and enduring relationships are protective factors that improve outcomes for care leavers. Staying Put can support participation in education, employment and training, strengthen emotional wellbeing, and reduce the likelihood of crisis-driven housing moves.

Considerations for local authorities

Local authorities should:

promote Staying Put as a positive option and discuss it as part of pathway planning well before a young person reaches the age of 18.

consider Staying Put alongside other accommodation pathways, recognising that young people develop independence at different rates.

work proactively with foster carers and young people to identify and address barriers to Staying Put arrangements.

ensure decisions are based on the young person’s needs, wishes and best interests.

monitor local demand and capacity and take steps to increase the availability of Staying Put arrangements where required.

clearly set out local Staying Put arrangements within the local offer for care leavers.

ensure robust contingency arrangements where there is a risk of a Staying Put arrangements ending in an unplanned way, including support to identify and address concerns early.

Supporting education, employment and training

Where a young person is participating in education, training or employment, local authorities should give particular consideration to the benefits of maintaining accommodation stability. Staying Put can provide the secure foundation young people need to focus on their studies, complete qualifications, sustain employment and build skills and confidence gradually, while maintaining the supportive relationships and networks that enable healthy interdependence.

Accommodation for care experienced young people in higher and further education

Stable, suitable accommodation is a foundation for educational success. For care leavers in further and higher education, housing support should go beyond simply providing somewhere to live.

Accommodation should provide the stability and security needed to participate fully in education, sustain relationships and support networks, and avoid housing disruption that can undermine attendance, attainment and wellbeing.

Local authorities should therefore ensure that accommodation planning is integrated with a young person’s pathway plan and educational aspirations, with housing needs considered early and reviewed as circumstances change.

Effective planning should extend beyond meeting this minimum statutory requirement. Unlike many of their peers, care leavers may not have a family home to return to during holidays or when courses end. Local authorities should therefore work with education and housing partners to prevent gaps in accommodation and support, ensuring access to safe, secure and suitable housing during term time, vacation periods and transitions into and out of education.

Local offers should clearly set out the accommodation and financial support available before, during and after study. This should include information on housing allowances, rent deposit and guarantor schemes, and year-round accommodation arrangements, including 365-day accommodation offers where available. They should also explain how care leavers studying outside their home local authority area will be supported and how continuity of accommodation will be maintained across local authority boundaries.

Crucially, accommodation planning should not end at graduation. Local offers should set out the housing advice, practical assistance and wider support available as care leavers complete their studies and move towards independent adulthood, with early planning to reduce the risk of housing instability or homelessness at the point of transition.

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

The following considerations can help prevent accommodation issues disrupting a care leaver’s education:

planning early: housing requirements should be identified through pathway planning before a young person starts or changes a course, including arrangements for term time, vacations, placement periods and the end of study

avoiding accommodation gaps: particular attention should be given to points at which accommodation may end unexpectedly or routinely, including the end of university or college terms, changes in course or institution, withdrawal from study and graduation. Contingency arrangements should be considered where there is a foreseeable risk of a gap

working with education providers: leaving care teams should develop effective links with universities, colleges and student accommodation services so that accommodation issues can be identified early and support coordinated where a care leaver is at risk of losing their accommodation

supporting care leavers studying away from home: the responsible local authority should maintain effective support where a young person studies in another area, including clarity about who the young person should contact if their accommodation becomes unsuitable or is at risk

considering the suitability of student accommodation: decisions should take account of the individual young person’s needs and circumstances, including whether accommodation provides appropriate stability and enables them to sustain their education and wider support networks

planning for course completion: pathway planning should anticipate what happens when student accommodation ends. Leaving care, housing and homelessness services should work together early enough to identify suitable onward accommodation and avoid graduation becoming a point of housing crisis

Staying Close

Purpose

The national rollout of the Staying Close duty through the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 represents a significant opportunity for local authorities to strengthen support for care-experienced young people and reduce the risk of homelessness.

From 2029, all local authorities will have a statutory duty to provide Staying Close support, including assistance with housing and access to wider services. By 2029, the programme will be rolled out nationally, with funding to build capacity through housing models that build connection around care leavers.

Through the Staying Close programme, local authorities will create housing options that build connection around young people. In order to receive Staying Close funding, local authorities must deliver a specific mental health support element and at least one of the approved housing support models – either supported by an external provider or as an in-house version:

a community-building housing project, such as the National House Project, Break, and similar others

supported lodgings

intensive family-based support (such as Shared Lives)

Safe, secure and suitable housing is the foundation for successful transitions to adulthood. Local authorities should use the implementation of Staying Close, alongside the new local offer duties, to strengthen housing pathways, improve joint working with housing partners, and ensure care leavers have a safe, secure and suitable long-term home.

The Department for Education will monitor local authority-level care leaver homelessness rates as a key performance indicator for the Staying Close programme, alongside delivery against agreed targets for additional care leavers moved into a suitable home through Staying Close.

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should begin preparing now by:

ensuring the personal adviser service is set up to support young people and give them the time they need for support and advice as they transition to adulthood

reviewing current housing pathways for care leavers and identifying gaps in provision

strengthening joint protocols between children’s services and housing departments

ensuring local offers clearly set out available accommodation options and housing support

expanding opportunities and support for care leavers to access Staying Put, their own tenancies, supported lodgings and other suitable housing options

embedding relationship-based practice and ensuring young people can maintain important connections as they move towards successful interdependence as adults

using data on homelessness, housing outcomes and service demand to inform local planning and commissioning

Family Finding

Family Finding programmes aim to ensure that children in care and care leavers have a positive, lasting network of family and trusted adults throughout their lives. They focus on supporting children and young people to reconnect with loved ones and build a network of familial and other close support.

An evaluation of DfE’s Family Finding, Befriending and Mentoring programme found that in Family Finding programmes most participants reported positive outcomes related to increased support network, stronger sense of identity, increased knowledge of their family, and repaired relationships. It also found that participants had a statistically significant increase of 2.2 additional connections.

As local authorities strengthen their support for care leavers through Staying Close, Local Offers and homelessness prevention activity, Family Finding programmes can provide a practical, evidence-based way to help young people build and maintain the relationships that underpin successful transitions to adulthood, stable housing and long-term wellbeing.

The Foundations – What Works Centre for Children & Families Reunification Practice Guidance aims to help families to stay together and get the help they need; children to be supported by their family network; and children in care and care leavers to have stable, loving homes.

Why it matters

Positive and enduring relationships are a key protective factor for care leavers. Strong support networks can help young people navigate challenges, reduce isolation, improve emotional wellbeing and strengthen resilience. These relationships are particularly important as young people move towards adulthood and can play a significant role in preventing homelessness and supporting stable housing outcomes.

Considerations for local authorities

Local authorities can implement Family Finding as part of their wider support offer for children in care and care leavers by:

participating in the Family Finding rollout across eligible local authorities

commissioning or delivering the Family Finding programmes within children’s social care services. Embedding Family Finding within pathway planning and preparation for adulthood

using these programmes to strengthen their approach to promoting enduring relationships and supporting care-experienced young people beyond the age of 18

Social housing

Social housing can play an important role in helping care-experienced young people achieve stable, sustainable housing and avoid homelessness. While decisions about social housing allocations remain at the discretion of local housing authorities, we expect local authorities to take the circumstances of care experienced young people into account when determining priority, as part of their wider corporate parenting responsibilities. Care leavers under 25 are exempt from local connection and residency tests in order to access social housing, and we strongly encourage local authorities to give care leavers living in their area who wish to remain the same level of priority as their own care leavers.​

Why social housing matters

For many care leavers, social housing can provide greater stability, affordability and security than other housing options. As part of a planned housing pathway, it can help young people establish independent lives, sustain tenancies, and reduce the risk of homelessness. Social housing is more appropriate for care experienced young people with lower support needs, whereas other accommodation options would be more appropriate for people with higher needs, such as supported accommodation.

A stable home provides the foundation for positive outcomes across education, employment, health and wellbeing, enabling young people to focus on building their futures rather than managing housing uncertainty.

Corporate parenting and allocation policies

Local authorities have discretion to determine how social housing is allocated within their area, in line with the statutory framework. As corporate parents, authorities should consider whether their allocation schemes adequately recognise the needs of care-experienced young people and support planned transitions from care to adulthood.

Many local authorities already provide care leavers with enhanced preference or a high level of priority within their allocation schemes, recognising both their vulnerability to homelessness and the role stable housing plays in improving long-term outcomes.

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should consider how allocation policies can support care leavers to access suitable accommodation at the right time. This includes considering:

whether care leavers receive appropriate priority within local allocation schemes

how housing pathways align with pathway planning and preparation for adulthood

how waiting time and housing register status are recognised and protected

how young people can progress towards independence without being disadvantaged by changes in assessment, eligibility or local processes

Setting clear expectations for waiting time and priority can provide greater certainty for young people and support smoother transitions into settled accommodation.

Supported accommodation

Supported accommodation is a vital component of an effective housing pathway for care leavers. When combined with strong relationships and tailored support, it can help young people who are ready to develop the skills, confidence and stability they need to sustain housing, avoid homelessness and thrive in adulthood. If a 16–17-year-old care leaver is placed in a supported accommodation provision, it must be Ofsted registered in line with the Supported Accommodation (England) Regulations 2023. Further information on supported accommodation can be found in the Guide to the supported accommodation regulations including quality standards.

Why supported accommodation matters

Many care leavers are not ready to move directly into fully independent accommodation when they leave care. Supported accommodation can help by combining suitable housing with tailored support to help young people develop the skills and confidence needed for adulthood.

The review of early deaths of care leavers, ‘You really are on your own’, published in August 2026, underscored the significant risks of isolation and the importance of not taking young people’s request for independence at face value. It is crucial that young people are supported to live interdependently, and are enabled and encouraged to understand the value of community and the risks of isolation. Young people should never feel pushed or pressured into independent living. Independent accommodation should only be used when it is identified as the right choice for the young person, based on consideration of the full range of the young person’s needs, including relationships.

The review asked directors of children’s services to look at the quality of the support and accommodation being provided to young care leavers in supported or semi-independent accommodation in their areas. Commissioning arrangements should be carefully assessed to ensure sensitive, skilled, and empathic support for 17- and 18-year-olds, who will often be experiencing significant changes across different aspects of their lives, and may be living on their own for the first time. A long-term view should be adopted to ensure young people have stability and are not just supported to transition into adulthood but are set up to thrive as young adults.

High-quality supported accommodation can help young people:

develop practical life skills, including budgeting, cooking and managing a tenancy

build confidence and resilience

access education, employment and training opportunities

maintain positive relationships and support networks

reduce the risk of homelessness, rough sleeping and housing instability

move successfully into longer-term accommodation when ready

Local authorities, personal advisers and supported accommodation providers should be aware of the October 2026 Housing Benefit reforms for supported housing residents. The changes align Housing Benefit rules more closely with Universal Credit, enabling young people to retain more of their income when taking up employment or increasing their working hours. This can help remove financial disincentives to work and support care leavers to build financial resilience while living in supported accommodation.

Developing a range of accommodation options

There is no single accommodation model that will meet the needs of all care leavers. Local authorities should work with housing providers and partners to develop a diverse range of accommodation options that reflect different levels of need and vulnerability. Children’s services should work with local housing authorities to ensure that the accommodation and support needs of care-experienced young people are considered within the Local Supported Housing Strategy and associated needs assessment, as required by the Supported Housing Regulatory Oversight Act 2023. Local housing authorities should ensure that children’s services are involved in the strategy’s development, oversight and review, to support wider strategic planning for supported housing as part of a joint corporate parenting approach.

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should:

review whether there is sufficient supported accommodation to meet local demand

ensure commissioning arrangements provide a range of options for care leavers with different needs

monitor housing outcomes and tenancy sustainment rates

monitor the number of unplanned moves from supported accommodation including evictions to help improve practice and ensure this is always a last resort

ensure care leavers receive ongoing practical and emotional support after moving into accommodation

ensure every placement is the most appropriate setting to meet the young person’s needs and keep them safe

Herefordshire

Benefits and positive outcomes from Herefordshire supported accommodation programme

Herefordshire’s supported accommodation programme provides a flexible and supportive pathway that helps care experienced young people transition successfully to independent living while reducing the risk of homelessness and tenancy breakdown. Through strong partnership working, tailored accommodation options, early housing planning, and dedicated tenancy sustainment support, young people receive the right level of assistance at the right time, with the reassurance of being able to step back into supported accommodation if needed.

Herefordshire has developed a structured supported accommodation pathway that helps care experienced young people move safely from supported settings into adulthood. Delivered jointly by children’s services and housing services, the model combines accommodation, tenancy sustainment support and multi-agency partnership working to prevent homelessness and improve housing stability.

The pathway offers a range of accommodation options, including intensive supported accommodation with 24-hour support, standard supported accommodation, transitional homes, and independent tenancies with floating support. Housing and support are tailored to individual needs, with flexibility for support levels to increase or decrease over time. Importantly, young people can move back into supported accommodation if an independent tenancy breaks down, providing a vital safety net, giving young people second and third chances and reducing overall homelessness for care leavers.

Housing planning begins from age 16, and is supported through a “Preparation for Adulthood Panel” process which reviews pathway planning, living skills accommodation matching, and includes the expertise of a dedicated housing personal adviser, who coordinates housing applications, tenancy sustainment, and multi-agency support to avoid breakdowns in housing arrangements and promotes early intervention. Specialist support is available for older young people with more complex needs.

Specialist support is available for young parents in collaboration with the Baby Steps offer ran by Home Start, and for separated young people. Achieved through positive local links with supported accommodation providers.

Strong governance underpins the model, including a strategic housing board, joint housing and pre-eviction protocols, and stability meetings when accommodation risks emerge. The strategic housing board helps plan ahead to overcome sufficiency challenges and enables greater connectivity to secure housing opportunities when the county is planning developments.

These arrangements enable early intervention, helping to prevent tenancy breakdown and homelessness before crises occur. The model demonstrates how providing tailored support, second chances and a range of accommodation options can help care experienced young people achieve sustainable housing outcomes despite wider challenges such as housing shortages and affordability pressures.

As a result, more young people maintain tenancies the first time they secure one.

Supported lodgings

Supported lodgings is a category under supported accommodation and is covered by the Supported Accommodation (England) Regulations 2023. Supported lodgings provides accommodation in the home of a trained host who offers both a room and practical and emotional support. Unlike other categories of supported accommodation, supported lodgings involve a young person living in a host’s home, where support is provided primarily through the host’s day-to-day guidance, encouragement and relationship-based support, rather than through a staffed residential environment.

Hosts help young people develop the skills, confidence and resilience needed for adulthood, while providing a stable and supportive home environment. Supported lodgings can be particularly suitable for care-experienced young people who are not yet ready to live independently but do not require the higher levels of support associated with residential or specialist provision.

Through the Staying Close programme, we are working with local authorities to expand care leavers’ access to supported lodgings provision and shared lives (or similar schemes). This will require strategic support from local authority leaders to plan long-term for recruitment and support for hosts.

Why local authorities should consider supported lodgings

Supported lodgings offer a number of benefits for care leavers. They:

provide a gradual and supported transition to adulthood

reduce the “cliff edge” often experienced when young people leave care

help young people build practical life skills, including budgeting, cooking, housekeeping and travel

support engagement with education, employment and training

promote emotional wellbeing and resilience

strengthen enduring relationships through trusted adult support

provide a cost-effective alternative to more intensive accommodation and crisis responses

Many supported lodgings placements are linked to fostering services, with some hosts being former foster carers, helping young people maintain stability and continuity of relationships.

Nearly half of care leavers remain in supported lodgings placements for 18 months or longer, providing a strong foundation for a successful move into independent living.

Considerations for local authorities

Local authorities should:

identify young people who may benefit from a family-based environment before they leave care

invest in the recruitment, training and retention of supported lodgings hosts

ensure robust matching processes based on the young person’s needs, aspirations and support requirements

embed relationship-based practice and focus on maintaining enduring relationships

Home for Good

Home for Good coordinates the Supported Lodgings National Network, bringing together around 150 local authority and independent schemes across England. Supported lodgings is a relationship-based intervention, rather than simply an accommodation offer, helping to reduce the cliff edge that many young people experience as they leave care.

Careful matching and personalised support are central to the model, with young people matched with hosts based on their individual needs and circumstances. Through everyday life within the home, hosts support young people to develop practical life skills such as budgeting, cooking, housekeeping and travel, alongside assistance with education, employment and training and emotional wellbeing. 90% of young people living in supported lodgings said it had helped them develop the confidence to live independently, while nearly half of care leavers remain in supported lodgings placements for 18 months or longer, providing a stable foundation from which to consider next steps.[footnote 6]

Supported lodgings can provide a cost-effective option, helping to prevent homelessness and reduce reliance on more expensive residential care, emergency accommodation and crisis interventions. Key to the model is prioritising relationship-based support, investing in host recruitment and careful matching, strong partnership working, and early move-on planning to ensure young people are well prepared for independence. Evidence from young people demonstrates the strength of the model, with 92% reporting that they feel safe in their supported lodgings home, 84% saying it feels like home, and 89% reporting a positive relationship with their host.[footnote 7]

Megan’s transition from residential care

Megan entered care aged five and experienced foster care before spending four years living in a children’s home. At 18, she moved into supported lodgings with a couple.

The transition was carefully planned. Megan met her prospective hosts several times and had three overnight stays before moving in. She said that although she had initially been nervous, by the time she moved in permanently she already knew her hosts and “had no worries about it”.

Moving from a children’s home, where staff were always present, into a quieter family home was a significant adjustment. Megan developed a particularly close relationship with one of her hosts, who supported her through family difficulties while encouraging her to become more independent. Megan described her host as someone she looks up to and can confide in, with support available when she needs it while still being encouraged to do things for herself.

At the time of the interview, Megan was planning to return to college to complete her maths qualification, with ambitions to work in care. She described supported lodgings as “a very good way to go” and said she would recommend it “100%”.

Lambeth

As part of a wider redesign of its housing pathway for care leavers, Lambeth developed a supported lodgings scheme to provide a family-based alternative to semi-independent accommodation. Delivered through a commissioned contract with Depaul UK (a youth homelessness charity that provides safe housing, supported lodgings, and transition programs for young people leaving the care system).

The service supports care leavers and other vulnerable young people through stable home environments, trusted adult relationships, and personalised support.

The model offers longer-term supported lodgings placements and emergency accommodation within host households. It is particularly intended for care leavers who would benefit from a family setting, vulnerable 16- and 17-year-olds requiring emergency accommodation, and young people needing consistent relationships and positive adult role models during their transition to adulthood.

The accommodation is complemented by support from hosts, personal advisers, social workers, and housing services, providing a more nurturing environment than larger accommodation settings. A key strength of the model is its relationship-based approach. Supported lodgings offers young people the opportunity to live in a family-style environment where hosts can provide day-to-day guidance, emotional support, and stability.

The scheme was commissioned for six placements at an annual cost of approximately £96,000. It was viewed as a relatively low-cost alternative to semi-independent accommodation. It also prevented homelessness and reduced reliance on more expensive accommodation and support arrangements.

A challenge for the model was in recruiting and retaining sufficient hosts, resulting in low occupancy levels and limiting overall value for money.

Lambeth’s experience is that supported lodgings can be a valuable accommodation option for care experienced young people, and its success depends on local market capacity, effective host recruitment, and maintaining high occupancy levels.

It is important to test local demand and provider capacity before large-scale commissioning, but while recognising the benefits that family-based, relationship-led accommodation can offer to young people moving towards independence.

Shared Lives

Shared Lives is a family-based accommodation and support model that provides care experienced young people with a stable home, trusted relationships, and practical support as they transition into adulthood. Rather than being centred on a property or tenancy, the model is built around carefully matched relationships between young people and trained Shared Lives carers, helping to reduce the ‘cliff edge’ many care leavers experience when they leave care.

Shared Lives schemes operate across 137 local authorities and the model is increasingly being used as a Staying Close pathway, particularly for young people leaving foster care, residential care, and supported accommodation.

The model has proven especially beneficial for young people with autism, learning disabilities, neurodiversity, complex trauma, and mental health needs, including those who may not meet adult social care thresholds but still require ongoing support.

Shared Lives has a strong focus on enduring relationships as a primary intervention. Young people receive personalised support with independent living skills, financial literacy, emotional wellbeing, education, employment and training, and community participation. The model promotes gradual transitions, strengthens family and community connections, and provides early intervention before difficulties escalate into homelessness.

Shared Lives supports nearly 1,500 18–25-year-olds nationally. In the last two years, over 180 new care leavers have been supported across 40 schemes. Reported outcomes include improved wellbeing, stronger trusting relationships, high participation in education, employment and training, and very high rates of housing stability.

Key advice for local authorities includes to start planning early, aligning housing, children’s services and adult social care, investing in specialist Shared Lives carers, co-producing services with young people, and creating flexible pathways that extend beyond age-based service boundaries.

Homelessness to forever home

Gracie faced homelessness at 17. Her social worker supported her into her Shared Lives arrangement and Gracie tells us that from there her life changed forever. Gracie is autistic and has mental health needs.

Gracie describes herself as bubbly and chatty. Relationships and friendships matter deeply to her, and feeling known as a whole person has been central to her experience. Gracie’s Shared Lives carer Maria has been especially important because she took time to understand Gracie, her autism, her background and story. This made Gracie feel important and supported in the right ways.

Within Shared Lives Gracie has a package of support, she lives with Shared Lives carers and has day support too, Gracie says these relationships are what has made the difference, “Shared Lives is my founded family”. Gracie works as an Ambassador with Shared Lives Plus and tells us that through the care in Shared Lives and employment opportunities her confidence has grown and she has achieved things she would have never thought possible, “Shared Lives has given me a second chance at life. I never thought I’d have people to call my family, a safe and happy home and a job that I love”.

Gracie has built her independence through Shared Lives and is now exploring options with her local team of moving out of a full-time arrangement into her own home. Gracie would continue to have Shared Lives day support with her current carer, maintaining this trusting relationship, stability and consistency.

Housing projects

These projects promise young people a long-term home, following preparation for care leavers by developing confidence, practical skills and strong networks. Weekly sessions allow care leavers to build social skills and life skills through facilitated group work. Care leavers support one another as they plan to move into their home and settle into a new phase of their life. The Department for Education is working with local authorities to make housing projects available for more care leavers through Staying Close. Evidence suggests these projects can:

Improve housing stability: Young people move into their own homes and can remain there long term, providing security and reducing housing instability after leaving care. The model is highly effective at helping care leavers maintain their accommodation. For example local House Projects delivered in collaboration with the National House Project report no tenancy breakdowns or evictions.

Strengthen belonging and reduce isolation: Young people leave care as part of a group, and report that these projects help them develop supportive peer networks that reduce isolation and provide ongoing emotional and practical support.

One young person said:

I love where I live, a place to call my own and I have done just that, I have all the facilities I need around me.[footnote 8]

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should:

explore opportunities to develop dedicated housing projects with housing associations and local providers

consider prioritising care leavers at greatest risk of homelessness

ensure housing projects are linked to personal adviser support, Staying Close services and wider wellbeing support

involve care-experienced young people in the design and review of specialist housing projects

ensure move-on routes are clear so that young people can progress into settled accommodation when ready

National House Project

The National House Project is a psychologically informed practice framework that supports care experienced young people to move into and sustain their own homes while developing the skills, confidence and relationships needed for successful adulthood.

The approach forms part of the wider range of accommodation pathways available to care leavers and aligns closely with the principles of Staying Close. It emphasises interdependence – supporting young people to develop the skills, knowledge and confidence to manage their own home while remaining connected to their communities, sustaining enduring relationships and knowing when and how to seek support.

Delivered in partnership with local authorities, housing providers and landlords, Local House Projects work strategically to unlock housing provision for care leavers, including by ringfencing housing association properties for them. Over a 6–9-month period, young people take part in groupwork and one-to-one support to complete an experiential, AQA-certificated programme.

This combines practical preparation for moving into their own home with activities that build confidence, strengthen relationships and support young people to become good tenants and active members of their communities.

Peer relationships are an important part of the approach, helping young people to develop a strong network of support that can continue beyond the formal programme.

Support does not end when a young person moves into their home. Young people have ongoing access to a safe environment and trusted staff, enabling them to seek help when difficulties arise and for as long as it is needed.

Local House Project staff also develop close working relationships with housing providers and landlords which is supported by biannual meetings where providers come together to share best practice and contribute to the iterative development of the House Project approach.

Housing staff can participate in steering groups and programme activities, creating opportunities to co-develop supportive responses when difficulties arise. This relationship-based approach can help reduce the risk of tenancy breakdown, eviction and homelessness and promote sustained tenancies.

Key evidenced outcomes

Outcomes include:

87% of young people said the House Project had supported them to live independently (CLNM Peer Evaluation 2021)

86.1% felt the House Project had helped prepare them to live in their own home (CLNM Peer evaluation 2023)

85% said being part of their Local House Project had improved their mental health (CLNM Peer evaluation 2023)

75% had safety plans and were involved in shaping them (CLNM Peer evaluation 2023)

nearly 9 in 10 reported improvements in managing their home and budgeting (CLNM Peer evaluation 2023)

Rees Foundation

The Rees Foundation is a housing provider offering accommodation with support in the West Midlands. The project was reviewed by Justin Rogers, Ian Thomas, and Philip Mendes in 2024 “Way beyond the care cliff: exploring a housing and support service for care experienced people over 25” (Journal of Children’s Services research). The findings reveal that care leavers often face a cliff edge when statutory support ends, resulting in risks such as homelessness and social isolation. The Rees Foundation’s approach, which includes ongoing emotional and practical support, plays a crucial role in fostering safety, stability, and hope among tenants.

Through mentoring, advocacy, financial grants, training opportunities, practical assistance and peer support, it helps care experienced adults navigate challenges, access opportunities and build resilience throughout adulthood. Rees Foundation seeks to ensure that individuals can access support whenever they need it, recognising that challenges relating to housing, employment, finances, and wellbeing can arise at any stage of life.

A key feature of the model is its focus on creating lasting networks of support and belonging. By connecting care experienced people with mentors, staff, volunteers and peer communities, the Rees Foundation helps tackle isolation and provides access to trusted relationships that can offer guidance, encouragement and practical help. Its approach supports the factors known to underpin successful tenancy sustainment, including social connection, emotional support and access to advice during periods of crisis or change. In doing so it demonstrates how lifelong, relationship-based support can help reduce the risk of homelessness and promote long-term stability, wellbeing and independence.

In 2025, Rees supported 2,306 people, responded to 2,929 enquiries and managed 1,317 crisis contacts. The foundation completed 373 focused needs assessments, supported 2,029 through Ask Jan, an emotional support service, reached around 300 people through virtual peer support groups and worked with 135 young people through Future Me, providing direct interventions to young people in the Midlands. Service figures can overlap because people often use more than one form of support; this joined-up journey is central to the approach.

Break

Break’s Staying Close, Staying Connected (SCSC) programme was developed to support young people leaving care through a combination of stable shared accommodation in the community and personalised transition support.

Delivered by Break in partnership with local authorities, the programme is co-produced with young people and helps them develop the skills, confidence and support networks needed for adulthood while reducing the risk of housing instability and homelessness.

A key feature of the model is its focus on maintaining and developing trusted relationships after leaving care. Understanding the impact of an individual’s trauma and experiences is the basis for tailored support.

Young people receive help with managing a tenancy, emotional wellbeing, life skills, education, employment and training, as well as access to mentoring and peer networks. Independent evaluations found improvements in housing stability, life skills, participation in education and employment, and overall wellbeing, making SCSC a widely recognised example of a relationship-based approach to supporting care leavers into adulthood.

The model recognises that housing stability depends on more than secure accommodation alone, emphasising that stable relationships and a trauma-informed approach are crucial for long-term stability. Common themes include peer support, tenancy sustainment, co-production, lifelong relationships, community connection and prevention of isolation.

The model includes an opportunity for young people to take on their SCSC tenancy when they are ready, so that the house they feel safe and comfortable in can become a home for as long as they want.

Building on this approach, Break continues to work with local authority and housing partners to explore ways of increasing choice, stability and long-term housing options for care leavers.

Stepping stone accommodation

Stepping-stone accommodation can help care leavers build skills and confidence gradually while maintaining access to practical support, reducing the risk of tenancy breakdown, homelessness and rough sleeping.

One young person said:

I think they should have their own training flats for care leavers to live in to gain skills they need to live independently.

Another said

I had a month in a practice flat in my local area which gave me a clear understanding of how important it is to budget and to have a good network of people supporting me.[footnote 9]

Stepping-stone accommodation refers to housing that offers greater independence than supported accommodation, while providing a level of ongoing support and oversight.

Models vary locally and may include:

self-contained flats with light-touch support

shared accommodation with visiting support

transitional accommodation delivered through housing associations or voluntary sector providers

ring-fenced accommodation specifically for care leavers

The aim is to provide a safe environment in which young people can develop the skills, confidence and experience needed to sustain a tenancy. Providers establishing this type of accommodation should be mindful of the parameters set out in The Renters’ Rights Act 2025, including the new ground for possession.

Considerations for local authorities children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should:

Consider including stepping-stone provision within their care leaver housing pathway and local offer.

Develop a range of accommodation options so young people can move through provision at a pace that reflects their needs and readiness.

Work with housing authorities, housing associations, supported accommodation providers and voluntary sector organisations to increase availability.

Ensure accommodation is linked to wider support, including Personal Adviser support, education, employment and wellbeing services.

The Housing Network

The Housing Network offers local authorities a practical housing pathway that can support care leavers to transition successfully from care into adulthood. Through safe, supported accommodation and its ‘Momentum’ pathway, care-experienced young people are provided with the stability, guidance and tailored support needed to develop the skills and confidence to sustain tenancies over the longer term. The pathway combines accommodation with personalised, trauma-informed support, recognising that many care leavers require more than housing alone to achieve positive outcomes. Support is tailored to individual needs and can include tenancy management, budgeting, wellbeing, education, training and employment, helping young people build skills and resilience. The Housing Network are commissioned by the local authority to provide step-up/step-down accommodation for those who are single homeless and families.

Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme

Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme - Centrepoint provides a stepping stone for young people, who find work and are ready to move from supported accommodation. The programme offers affordable, self-contained studio homes, where young people pay just one-third of their gross annual salary in rent.

An example of this stepping stone housing pathway is Reuben House in Peckham, London, Centrepoint’s first Independent Living scheme. It provides 33 self-contained studio apartments and has become the blueprint for Centrepoint’s wider national model. Independent Living helps young people aged 18 to 25 to develop the practical skills needed for independent adulthood, including managing a tenancy, budgeting, sustaining employment and building savings.

Rents are linked to income and tenancies available for up to five years, so young people have the time and stability to establish themselves before moving into permanent housing.

The Independent Living programme offers young people an affordable stepping stone between supported housing and the private rented sector. It provides local authorities with options for young people who find work, want to move on from supported housing, but cannot find an affordable rent on their salaries.

Centrepoint’s Independent Living homes increase the volume of genuinely affordable housing for young people providing a sustainable route out of homelessness.

Reunification support

Where safe and appropriate, reunification support can help care-experienced young people strengthen, rebuild or sustain relationships with family members and wider support networks. As part of a wider housing pathway, reunification can contribute to housing stability, strengthen enduring relationships, and reduce the risk of homelessness by increasing the number of people a young person can turn to during times of crisis. This aligns with the emphasis on trusted adults, support networks and relationship-based practice across care leaver reforms.

Young care experienced parents may require additional support to access and sustain suitable accommodation while involved in pre-proceedings, care proceedings, or when working towards reunification with their children. Local authorities should ensure that housing instability does not become an unnecessary barrier to family outcomes. Effective support requires early coordination between housing services, leaving care teams, and children’s services, to identify accommodation needs, secure appropriate housing, and ensure that housing circumstances are considered separately from assessments of parenting capacity.

Reunification support involves helping young people safely reconnect with parents, siblings, wider family members or other significant adults where this is in their best interests. This may include:

Family mediation and relationship-building support.

Practical support to maintain family contact.

Support to resolve conflict and strengthen communication.

Assessment of family networks as part of pathway planning.

Use of Family Group Conferences and wider family network approaches.

Practical assistance to help young people access family support during housing difficulties.

Reunification is not about returning a young person to an unsafe environment. Instead, it seeks to strengthen positive relationships and support networks that can improve resilience and reduce isolation. There also needs to be strong contingency planning, should family member(s) or friend no longer be willing or able to accommodate the young person.

Considerations for local authorities

Local authorities should:

Consider family and relationship networks from an early stage of pathway planning.

Identify opportunities to safely strengthen family relationships before a young person leaves care.

Use family group decision-making and mediation approaches where appropriate.

Ensure Personal Advisers routinely discuss family and support networks with care leavers.

Recognise reunification support as a homelessness prevention intervention, not solely a social care intervention.

Maintain a focus on safeguarding and the wishes of the young person throughout the process.

Draw on the Foundations – What Works Centre for Children & Families Reunification Practice Guidance to inform local policy, practice and workforce development.

Sheffield Roundabout’s reunification support

Roundabout is one of South Yorkshire’s largest youth homelessness organisations, delivering a model of prevention, accommodation, and support. It prioritises early intervention, family-based solutions, and preventing homelessness before crisis point.

It offers a range of accommodation, including emergency hostels, crash-pad provision, supported and semi-independent housing, dispersed accommodation, rapid rehousing, resettlement services, and specialist provision for care leavers, refugees and apprentices through its Future Builders programme. The pathway enables young people to access support matched to their needs while developing life skills. Roundabout complements Sheffield’s care leaver pathway by providing specialist accommodation, tenancy sustainment and crisis prevention support alongside existing options such as Staying Put arrangements, training flats, and priority social housing access.

A key element of Roundabout’s prevention work is Talk It Out (Mediation), a family mediation service for young people aged 13 to 24. Using conflict coaching and family mediation, the service provides up to 13 sessions and successfully prevents homelessness in 94% of cases, helping improve communication, resilience, and family relationships. Additional support includes housing advice, benefits support, budgeting, employment and skills programmes, counselling, mental health support, advocacy, life-skills development and tenancy sustainment services to reduce repeat homelessness.

Private rented sector

The private rented sector (PRS) can play a valuable role in meeting the accommodation needs of care leavers, particularly in areas where social housing supply is limited. When combined with appropriate support, this accommodation can provide stable housing and help care leavers build skills and resilience as they transition into adulthood.

Use of PRS can increase the range of housing options available to care leavers by providing access to suitable accommodation where social housing supply is constrained and reduce the use of temporary, emergency or unsuitable accommodation.

Successful PRS pathways often include:

Tenancy preparation and life skills support.

Rent deposit, rent in advance, or rent guarantor schemes.

Ongoing tenancy sustainment support.

Mediation and landlord engagement services.

Practical support to access benefits and manage finances.

However, care leavers may face particular barriers to accessing the PRS, including affordability, lack of tenancy history, limited savings for deposits, and concerns from landlords about renting to young people.

Children’s services should develop any PRS offer in partnership with the local housing authority, drawing on their expertise in local private rented markets, existing relationships with landlords and letting agents, and role in supporting checks on property suitability, safety and quality.
