This joint approach can help ensure that PRS options for care leavers are realistic, safe, affordable and appropriately supported as part of the wider housing pathway.

Considerations for local authority children’s services and housing departments

Local authorities should:

Develop strong partnerships with private landlords, letting agents and housing providers.

Consider rent deposit, rent guarantee and rent bond schemes to improve access.

Ensure care leavers receive support to understand tenancy rights and responsibilities.

Provide practical support with budgeting, managing bills and maintaining a tenancy.

Identify young people who may require additional support before moving into the PRS.

Ensure private rented sector accommodation is safe, suitable and affordable.

Use pathway planning to prepare young people well in advance of a move into accommodation.

Link PRS accommodation with wider support services, including Staying Close, Personal Adviser support, education, employment and wellbeing services.

Deposit schemes and rent guarantors

Many care-experienced young people are unable to provide a cash deposit, access a suitable guarantor, or meet upfront rental costs, despite being ready to manage and sustain a tenancy.

A rent guarantor and deposit scheme can help care leavers overcome these barriers, which they can face when trying to access private rented accommodation. By offering these schemes, local authorities can help care leavers to access a wider range of safe and suitable housing options, thus reducing the risk of homelessness, and supporting a more stable transition to adulthood.

The Barnardo’s report The Case for a National Rent Guarantor and Deposit Scheme for Care Leavers Aged 18–24 in England (December 2023) highlighted that such schemes, particularly when combined with affordability checks, landlord engagement, and early intervention when difficulties arise, can all improve tenancy sustainment. They highlight the positive results of schemes, such as that offered by Kent Country Council.

Kent County Council

Kent County Council operates a combined rent guarantor and deposit scheme through its leaving care service to help care leavers access private rented accommodation when they are unable to provide a personal guarantor.

Applications to the scheme are assessed through affordability and sustainability checks, including reviews of income, bank statements, and tenancy details. Once approved, the local authority can act as guarantor for up to one year, which can be repeated if the first year has been successful and if the young person remains under age 25 and open to the service. It also covers rent only but not damages. Applicants should be working at least 8 hours a week to be guaranteed. The local authority may also provide rent in advance and tenancy deposits. Landlords are encouraged to notify the council promptly of any rent arrears so that support can be provided before difficulties escalate.

The scheme supports around 12-15 care leavers each year. Kent reports that it has enabled young people to secure tenancies that might otherwise have been inaccessible, sustain accommodation, and avoid homelessness. Financial risks to the local authority have remained low, with only a small number of defaults requiring payment and costs of approximately £6,000 over recent years.

A key reason for the scheme’s success is that it is not simply a financial guarantee. Kent combines guarantor and deposit support with robust affordability assessments, management oversight, integration with leaving care services, strong landlord relationships, and early intervention when tenancy difficulties emerge.

The local authority received eighteen applications from August 2025 to August 2026. Of these requests, the local authority negotiated to a position of no requirement for a guarantor for two of these young people. Two applications were rejected due to poor supporting evidence, such as clear bank details on expenditure. The local authority agreed to be guarantor for fourteen young people, with the total liability being £101,364. Of these fourteen, there has been one issue of non-payment of rent lasting two months and totalling £1,430. The local authority is negotiating with the young person and landlord to have the payments made up by the young person when this becomes possible.

Part 4: Examples of housing pathways

The information below is intended to provide insights for local authorities, their partners, and other relevant organisations. The examples presented are not intended to be exhaustive but offer potential learning and a range of approaches that have been adopted by different areas.

Hull

Benefits and positive outcomes

Hull’s pathway combines early planning, consistent support and a range of accommodation options to help care leavers achieve stable, independent living. Its preventative approach has delivered strong outcomes, including high rates of homelessness prevention, tenancy sustainment, suitable accommodation and participation in education, employment and training.

The case for implementation

This model shows how close partnership working across housing and children’s services can prevent homelessness and reduce reliance on crisis responses. By identifying needs early and providing coordinated support, local authorities can improve outcomes for care leavers while strengthening their corporate parenting offer.

Hull has developed a mature and highly integrated housing pathway for care experienced young people. At the centre of this is a targeted youth support accommodation hub, which acts as a single point of access for housing advice, homelessness prevention, supported accommodation, emergency accommodation, and move-on planning for care experienced young people age 16-25.

A key strength of the model is the close partnership between housing services, children’s social care, leaving care services, and targeted youth support. Weekly transition panels, shared decision-making, and a strong corporate parenting culture, all help ensure that housing needs are identified early and addressed through coordinated support.

Planning for adulthood begins from age 16½, with personal advisers allocated from age 17, and accommodation needs regularly reviewed as part of transition planning.

Hull’s pathway is built around a continuum of support, comprising five stages:

Advice and Information

Prevention and Early Help

Crisis Prevention and Relief

Accommodation and Support

Sustainable Housing

Young people can access a range of accommodation options depending on their needs, including Staying Put arrangements and supported lodgings. Hull also operates supported accommodation, their shared tenancies project (which has 105 places across 43 properties), 10 gateway units, and 21 specialised supported housing units.

The model places a strong emphasis on prevention and continuity of support. Young people retain the same personal adviser throughout their transition to adulthood, helping to build trusted relationships, and providing consistent support.

Supported accommodation offers practical help with life skills, budgeting, tenancy management, and access to education, training and employment opportunities, while specialist pathways are available for young people with higher levels of need. Suitability is assessed holistically, taking account of affordability, stability, wellbeing, support networks, and access to education, employment and local services.

The local authority funds university accommodation and provides support with student finance, bursaries, UCAS applications and holiday accommodation. There are currently 24 care leavers attending university.

Hull reports strong outcomes from their approach, including homelessness prevention rates of over 90%, no use of bed and breakfast accommodation through a targeted youth support pathway for more than four years, high levels of tenancy sustainment, and positive education, employment and training outcomes.

The local authority reports that 94% of care leavers aged 19-21 are living in suitable accommodation. The model demonstrates the value of early planning, integrated working, a diverse range of accommodation options or their young people, and a sustained focus on homelessness prevention - rather than crisis intervention.

Hounslow

Benefits and positive outcomes

Hounslow’s integrated housing pathway delivers better housing stability and stronger transitions to adulthood for its care experienced young people. Through early planning, coordinated multi-agency support, and a graduated accommodation pathway, young people are able to build skills and confidence at the right pace while receiving practical support to sustain tenancies. The model has contributed to high tenancy sustainment rates, increased access to social housing and low levels of homelessness, reducing the need for crisis intervention. Positive outcomes are evidenced by zero evictions out of 235 tenancies over the past few years, demonstrating that care leavers are being supported to sustain their tenancies and achieve positive housing outcomes.

The case for implementation

The approach provides a clear, preventative framework that strengthens corporate parenting responsibilities and improves outcomes for care leavers. By aligning housing and children’s services through formal partnership arrangements, local authorities can identify risks earlier, prevent tenancy breakdown and make more effective use of limited housing resources. The model demonstrates how coordinated support and flexible housing options can improve long-term housing stability while reducing demand for costly emergency accommodation.

Hounslow local authority has developed an integrated housing pathway for its care experienced young people, which is underpinned by a formal protocol between the housing department and children’s services. It clearly sets out the shared responsibilities and coordinated approach to supporting young people leaving care. The pathway is delivered through a whole-system partnership involving children’s services, housing services, personal advisers, commissioned providers (such as Settle, which supports young people to transition into their first home, providing one-to-one coaching for life skills, managing money, and keeping a tenancy) and the YMCA, Hounslow’s commissioned supported living service, the joint move-on panel, and senior leaders.

The model has a graduated accommodation pathway which enables young people to progress through different levels of support as their skills and confidence develop. This includes supported accommodation, semi-independent accommodation, and step-down provision, before progressing to independent housing where appropriate.

The pathway is principally social housing-led, reflecting the local authority’s corporate parenting commitment to providing care leavers with access to stable and affordable housing. The local authority in recognising future housing supply pressures is also exploring additional private rented sector pathways, to complement existing social housing routes and provide greater flexibility in meeting future demand.

The pathway begins before a young person moves on from care. It places a strong emphasis on early planning, tenancy sustainment and homelessness prevention. Accommodation needs are considered as part of wider pathway planning, with readiness assessments and multi-agency decision-making helping to ensure that housing options are matched to the young person’s needs, skills and confidence.

Young people are supported through every stage of their journey, with access to pre-tenancy preparation, practical life-skills development, mentoring, education, employment and training support, and intensive tenancy sustainment services.

The model’s focus is on preventing tenancy breakdown before problems escalate. Housing and children’s services operate as an integrated system, enabling young people experiencing difficulties to access practical support, mentoring, tenancy advice, and additional case oversight.

Complex cases are escalated through governance arrangements and the joint move-on panel, ensuring that housing risks are identified early and addressed through coordinated action.

The local authority reports a number of positive outcomes from their approach, including significant numbers of care leavers moving into social housing tenancies, low levels of homelessness presentations, high tenancy sustainment rates, improved forward planning of housing transitions and better identification of future housing need.

The model demonstrates how strong partnership working, formal joint protocols, a range of accommodation pathways, effective tenancy sustainment support and ongoing support beyond age 21 can improve housing stability, prevent homelessness and reduce the need for crisis interventions or emergency accommodation.

Hounslow experienced a backlog in 2023/24 and 2024/25 so strengthened its integrated housing pathway, creating a more consistent flow of accommodation opportunities for care leavers.

While some challenges remain, the pathway is now well established and operating effectively, supported by a steady supply of local authority and Housing Association accommodation, with further provision expected from 2026/27 onwards.

Devon’s improvement programme

Benefits and positive outcomes from Devon’s improvement programme

Devon’s improvement programme has created a more consistent, coordinated and preventative housing system for care experienced young people across the county. Through stronger partnership working, a county-wide housing protocol, expanded supported accommodation, enhanced access to social and private rented housing, and improved tenancy sustainment arrangements, care leavers are better supported to secure and maintain suitable homes. The programme has strengthened early transition planning, reduced the risk of homelessness and tenancy breakdown, increased housing options, and improved support for young people with differing levels of need.

The case for implementation

Devon’s experience demonstrates that reducing care leaver homelessness requires whole-system reform rather than isolated interventions. By bringing together housing, children’s services, accommodation providers, and senior leaders, around shared objectives, local authorities can create more coherent housing pathways, improve consistency of practice, and address barriers more effectively. A strong focus on prevention, governance, tenancy sustainment and early planning can improve outcomes for care experienced young people, while reducing reliance on crisis responses and making better use of limited housing resources.

Devon local authority has undertaken a significant long-term improvement programme to strengthen housing pathways for care-experienced young people and reduce the risk of homelessness as they transition into adulthood.

Operating across most of Devon (excluding Plymouth and Torbay) the programme has required close collaboration between Devon County Council, eight district councils, housing associations, supported accommodation providers, landlords, personal advisers, and Devon Home Choice (a shared social housing register and bidding system used by local authorities across Devon, through which care leavers can apply for affordable social rented homes, with support from personal advisors and local housing teams).

Devon’s improvement journey has been led by key partners, including children’s services, housing services, and commitment from senior leaders. The active involvement of the county council chief executive and district council chief executives has been particularly important in driving change, overcoming barriers, and maintaining a shared focus on improving outcomes for care leavers.

The programme emerged in response to growing concerns about housing instability, tenancy breakdown, increasing numbers of young people entering care, and the challenges of delivering a consistent housing offer across eight district councils.

Housing shortages, rural geography, and fragmented local arrangements often made it difficult for care leavers to secure and sustain suitable accommodation.

As no single intervention could address the challenges, the local authority adopted a system-wide approach to reform. It included developing a county-wide housing protocol established across eight district councils. The protocol has created greater consistency in practice, clarified responsibilities, and strengthened partnership working across the housing and children’s services system.

Devon also introduced reforms to improve accommodation options and support pathways. Care leavers receive enhanced priority through the Devon Home Choice allocations system, with support available through youth enquiry service centres in Exeter, Barnstaple and Newton Abbot.

Senior leaders review housing issues affecting care leavers, enabling barriers and challenges to be escalated and resolved quickly. A major development has been the expansion of supported accommodation, increasing from 17 to 58 providers, creating greater choice, flexibility and capacity.

The local authority has also strengthened eviction prevention and tenancy sustainment arrangements through escalation procedures, provider reviews, and earlier intervention where placements are at risk of breaking down.

Devon substantially expanded its Staying Put offer, enabling more young people to remain with former foster carers beyond the age of 18. The authority has also developed its Staying Close provision, providing intensive support and accommodation options for young people leaving residential care who have higher levels of need and vulnerability.

Access to the private rented sector has been strengthened through landlord engagement, rent guarantor schemes, and deposit support. This has helped build landlord confidence in renting to care leavers, while expanding the range of housing options available.

Devon has also introduced a pathway planning forum to encourage earlier transition planning, improve coordination between services, and ensure young people are better prepared for independent living.

Significant challenges currently remain as Devon continues to operate across a large and predominantly rural area, where housing supply is limited and communities can be geographically dispersed.

Care leavers may face difficulties when moving from supported accommodation into their own tenancies, while affordability pressures and limited housing stock continue to restrict available options. The work to date has though created a more coherent and effective housing pathway for care experienced young people than existed previously.

The key lesson Devon has derived is that to reduce care leaver homelessness it requires more than increasing accommodation supply. Success depends on system-wide reform, strong governance, collaborative leadership, and a shared commitment to supporting young people before housing crises occur.

By focusing on prevention, preparation for adulthood and flexible support options, the local authority has strengthened outcomes for care experienced young people and created a more sustainable housing pathway for them into adulthood.
